newsitem.title: UK: British markets greet election manifestos with a yawn.
newsitem.headline: British markets greet election manifestos with a yawn.

text.p: British election fever hotted up this week as the ruling Conservative and opposition Labour parties launched rival manifestos, but London's financial markets greeted their policy promises with a resounding yawn.

Both parties claimed they were offering radical programmes for Britain's future, but Labour's election pledges failed to ruffle any financial market feathers on Thursday and the Conservative manifesto met with equal disdain on Wednesday.

Analysts said Labour's blueprint had contained no surprises to set traders' pulses racing, while the Conservatives' promises were ignored because markets feel the party has little chance of winning the May 1 general election. Labour is well ahead in opinion polls and widely expected to form the next government.

Rather than being gripped by the election campaign, traders were instead looking across the Atlantic for inspiration -- concerns about U.S. interest rates have dominated markets all week and dealers are on tenterhooks ahead of Friday's key U.S. payrolls data. Analysts said the election was a mere sideshow.
"It's as dull as ditchwater," said Tom Rayner, gilts analyst at SocGen.

"The result of the election is so clear now...that we can ignore what the Conservatives have put in their manifesto because it doesn't matter," he said. "Even now we've seen Labour's manifesto, nothing's changed to push the market one way or the other."

"New Labour", looking to claim the political middle ground, repeated in its policy blueprint the party's pledges to stick to the current government's spending targets for two years and maintain the Conservatives' 2.5-percent inflation target. It promised not to raise income tax.
Analysts said the manifesto contained no changes to the party's existing economic pledges. The crucial issue was whether they stuck to these promises if elected, they said.

"The overall thrust of Labour's manifesto seems to have been to be as unexciting and unsurprising as possible and that in itself minimised any market interest," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.

Gilts showed no reaction to Labour's proposals and sterling also shrugged off any impact. The stock market was equally unexcited -- although the FTSE 100 blue-chip index fell, analysts said fears of another Wall Street tumble were to blame.

"I don't think there was a great deal expected from the manifesto," a share dealer said. "They have kept things very sketchy." He said the FTSE had largely ignored the document, although shares may have been slighty encouraged by an absence of any nasty surprises.

Labour has long said it will introduce a windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities if it wins the election, and this has hit utilities shares in recent months. But the manifesto contained no new details about the proposal.

"The market will concentrate on Labour's spending plans, and specifically its windfall tax plans," the share dealer said. "But they didn't give much away and that'll leave the market with a bit of uncertainty."
Markets have traditionally regarded Labour with suspicion, although some of this animosity may have been dispelled by the party's move towards the political centre-ground.
But analysts say a Labour victory has long been discounted and, barring any last-minute bombshells, markets are unlikely to get worked up by the election battle.

"We're almost into overkill on the election -- it's on every news programme and in every newspaper," Rayner said. "But we're going to have to see the polls swinging massively to the Conservatives to see the market getting geed up."
Only such a swing would induce markets to regard the Conservative manifesto and its centrepiece of tax cuts seriously, analysts say.
Although a late surge in Conservative support would have been a bullish signal for markets in previous elections, analysts say the reverse could be true this time.

A Conservative fightback would raise the spectre of a hung parliament, where no party won overall control, and analysts say a smooth cruise to victory by Labour would be more positive for markets than late signs that the race was getting close.

"No news is good news for the currency at the moment and as long as the economic data stays as strong as it is, the focus is more on post-election interest-rate rises," one foreign exchange trader said. "Neither party can avoid that reality."
